title: 109 In vitro and in situ digestibility of warm-season grass and legume mixtures in the Southeast
content:
Abstract
Warm-season annual forages are highly digestible and commonly used to interseed within permanent perennial pastures, providing cattle with high-quality nutrition without requiring concentrate feed supplementation. These forages can be utilized during the dormancy of cool-season forage to potentially increase average daily gain in cattle. This study aimed to evaluate the in vitro and in situ dry matter digestibility of mixtures of crabgrass (Digitaria sanguinalis) and pearl millet (Pennisetum glaucum; G) and crabgrass and pearl millet with a 30% inclusion rate of forage soybeans (Glycine max; G+L). Forages were collected in June, July, August, and September of 2021 and 2022 and composited across years within month. Two ruminally cannulated steers from the Stanley P. Wilson Beef Teaching Center (Auburn, AL) were used to conduct the digestibility analyses. In vitro analysis was conducted using the batch culture method, while the in situ was performed using reverse incubation. For both methods, samples were incubated for 2, 4, 8, 12, 24, 48 and 72 h. Results from the in vitro study indicated differences in dry matter digestibility of G for among all months (P < 0.001). June G samples had 63.5% digestibility and September samples had 45.9% digestibility (P < 0.001). These results are as expected with declining digestibility as forage matures later in the season. Digestibility also differed across incubation times (P < 0.001), with digestion plateauing at 48 h. For G+L, there was also an effect of month (P = 0.015), with August and September being less digestible than June or July. Results from the in situ study indicated the rate of digestion (kd) did not differ (P = 0.359) among months for G. There was, however, a difference among months (P = 0.037) for G+L in which the kd for June was greater than any other month. The potentially degradable fraction (D) was greatest (P < 0.001) in July from G, but there was no difference (P = 0.195) among months from G+L. For both G and G+L, the undegradable fraction (U) was increased with advancing maturity (P < 0.001). Overall, these studies provide valuable insights into the digestibility and fiber degradation rate of warm-season annual forages. The findings emphasize how forage composition and maturity contribute to improving forage management strategies for livestock production systems.
